q: What is opportunity cost?
r: The value of the next best alternative that is given up
Every choice means giving up something else.
w: The total dollar price paid when buying something
Price is only part of the cost of a choice.
The extra fee charged when ordering at a store
Fees are not what opportunity cost measures.
The profit a business earns after paying expenses
That describes net income, not a trade-off.

q: Why does scarcity force people to make choices?
r: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
People cannot have everything they want.
w: Governments ban most products from being made
Scarcity exists without any bans.
Businesses refuse to produce enough goods
Scarcity does not come from business refusal.
Money has no value in modern economies
Money still has value.

q: Which of the following is a factor of production?
r: Labor, which is the work done by people
Land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship are the four factors.
w: Inflation, which is a general rise in prices
Inflation is a result, not an input.
Profit, which is money left after all costs
Profit is a reward, not an input.
Demand, which is the desire to buy goods
Demand is a market force, not an input.

q: What does the factor of production called 'capital' refer to?
r: Tools, machinery and buildings used to make goods
Capital is human-made resources used in production.
w: The money a person keeps in a savings account
In economics, capital means productive goods.
The natural resources found beneath the ground
Those are land resources.
The skills that an entrepreneur must have
That is entrepreneurship or human capital.

q: What is an entrepreneur?
r: A person who organizes resources and takes the risk of starting a business
Entrepreneurs bring land, labor and capital together.
w: A person who works for a fixed wage in a store
That describes an employee.
A person who collects taxes for the government
That describes a tax official.
A person who lends money to businesses
That describes a lender.

q: Which choice best illustrates a trade-off?
r: Spending an evening studying instead of working a shift
Time spent one way cannot be spent another way.
w: Buying a gift with money found on the sidewalk
Nothing is given up when the money is free.
Receiving a prize for winning a contest
A prize involves no sacrifice.
Inheriting a house from a relative
An inheritance involves no trade-off.

q: A student can spend Saturday either earning $80 at a job or attending a free workshop. What is the opportunity cost of attending the workshop?
r: The $80 that could have been earned at the job
The best alternative given up is the lost wages.
w: The $0 admission price to the workshop
The workshop is free, but the day is not.
The $160 that two Saturdays would earn
Only one Saturday is being given up.
The cost of the workshop's materials
The materials are not part of the choice.

q: What does the law of demand state?
r: As price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal
Buyers purchase less when a good costs more.
w: As price rises, quantity demanded rises too
This reverses the law.
As income rises, prices must always rise
The law concerns price and quantity.
As supply rises, demand must also rise
Supply and demand are separate forces.

q: What does the law of supply state?
r: As price rises, quantity supplied rises, other things equal
Producers offer more when they can earn more.
w: As price rises, quantity supplied falls
This reverses the law.
As demand falls, prices always rise
The law concerns price and quantity supplied.
As costs rise, producers always make more
Higher costs usually reduce supply.

q: At the equilibrium price, what is true about the market?
r: Quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
No shortage or surplus remains at that price.
w: The government has set a fixed price
Equilibrium comes from market forces.
Producers earn zero revenue
Revenue is still earned at equilibrium.
Consumers stop buying altogether
Buyers still purchase at equilibrium.

q: If the price of a product is above equilibrium, what results?
r: A surplus, because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Sellers have unsold goods and tend to lower prices.
w: A shortage, because buyers want more than is available
A shortage occurs when price is below equilibrium.
No change, because prices never affect markets
Prices drive market adjustment.
A permanent monopoly for one seller
A surplus does not create a monopoly.

q: If the price of a product is below equilibrium, what results?
r: A shortage, because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Buyers compete for limited goods and prices tend to rise.
w: A surplus, because sellers have extra goods
A surplus occurs when price is above equilibrium.
A tax refund for all buyers
Prices do not cause tax refunds.
A decrease in the number of buyers
A low price attracts more buyers.

q: Which event would shift the demand curve for gasoline to the left?
r: A sharp rise in the popularity of electric cars
Fewer buyers want gasoline at every price.
w: A fall in the cost of crude oil
That would shift supply, not demand.
A new refinery opening near a large city
That would shift supply to the right.
A cold winter that raises heating needs
That affects heating fuel, not gasoline demand.

q: Which event would shift the supply curve for bread to the left?
r: A rise in the price of wheat flour
Higher input costs reduce supply at every price.
w: A rise in consumer income
That affects demand.
A new fad diet that favors bread
That affects demand.
A drop in the price of bakery ovens
That would raise supply.

q: What is a substitute good?
r: A product that can replace another when its price changes
Tea and coffee are common substitutes.
w: A product that is used together with another
That describes a complement.
A product that is only sold by one company
That describes a monopoly product.
A product that has no price at all
Substitutes have prices.

q: What is a complementary good?
r: A product that is used together with another product
Printers and ink cartridges are complements.
w: A product that can replace another product
That describes a substitute.
A product that is given away for free
Complements are not necessarily free.
A product that is sold only abroad
Location does not define a complement.

q: The price of hot dogs rises sharply. What is the likely effect on the demand for hot dog buns?
r: Demand for buns falls, because the two goods are complements
Fewer hot dogs bought means fewer buns needed.
w: Demand for buns rises, because the goods are substitutes
Buns and hot dogs are not substitutes.
Demand for buns is unchanged, because the goods are unrelated
The goods are closely related.
Supply of buns rises immediately
The change described affects demand, not supply.

q: What is elasticity of demand?
r: How strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change
Elastic goods show large changes in buying.
w: How quickly a business can hire new workers
That concerns labor markets.
How much a product costs to make
That concerns production cost.
How long a product lasts before it breaks
That concerns durability.

q: Which good is likely to have inelastic demand?
r: Insulin for a person with diabetes
There is no good substitute, so buyers keep buying.
w: A particular brand of potato chips
Many substitutes make demand elastic.
A restaurant meal on a weeknight
Buyers can easily skip it.
A luxury vacation package
Buyers can postpone luxuries.

q: If demand for a product is elastic and its price rises, what happens to total revenue?
r: Total revenue falls, because quantity drops by a larger percentage
Buyers cut purchases more than the price increase.
w: Total revenue rises, because every buyer pays more
Quantity falls too much for revenue to rise.
Total revenue stays exactly the same
Revenue changes when demand is elastic.
Total revenue doubles automatically
There is no such rule.

q: What is the term for the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good?
r: Marginal utility
It usually declines as more units are consumed.
w: Total revenue
That is the money earned from sales.
Opportunity cost
That is the value of the best alternative.
Fixed cost
That is a cost that does not change with output.

q: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that:
r: Each additional unit consumed gives less added satisfaction
The fifth slice of pizza satisfies less than the first.
w: Each additional unit consumed gives more added satisfaction
This reverses the law.
Total satisfaction always falls with each unit
Total satisfaction may still rise.
Prices always fall as consumption rises
The law does not set prices.

q: What does gross domestic product (GDP) measure?
r: The total value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period
It is the broadest measure of output.
w: The total amount of money in all bank accounts
GDP measures output, not savings.
The number of people who have jobs
That is employment.
The average price of consumer goods
That is a price index.

q: Which is a final good for GDP purposes?
r: A loaf of bread bought by a family for dinner
Final goods are sold to the end user.
w: Flour bought by a bakery to make bread
That is an intermediate good.
Yeast bought by a bakery for dough
That is an intermediate good.
Sugar bought by a factory for cookies
That is an intermediate good.

q: Why are intermediate goods left out of GDP?
r: Counting them would count the same value more than once
Their value is already in the final price.
w: Intermediate goods are always illegal
They are legal.
They have no economic value
They have value.
They are produced only in other countries
They are produced at home too.

q: What are the four components of GDP in the expenditure approach?
r: Consumption, investment, government spending and net exports
C + I + G + (X - M).
w: Wages, rent, interest and profit
Those are income-approach components.
Land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
Those are factors of production.
Supply, demand, price and quantity
Those are market concepts.

q: Consumption is $700, investment $150, government spending $200, exports $90 and imports $110. What is GDP?
w: This adds imports instead of subtracting them.
This ignores net exports.
This adds exports only.

q: What is the difference between nominal GDP and real GDP?
r: Real GDP is adjusted for inflation; nominal GDP is not
Real GDP compares output across years fairly.
w: Nominal GDP excludes government spending; real GDP includes it
Both include government spending.
Real GDP counts only exports; nominal GDP counts imports
Neither counts only exports.
There is no difference between the two
Inflation adjustment makes them differ.

q: Which statement describes a recession?
r: A significant decline in economic activity lasting several months or more
Output, income and jobs typically fall.
w: A short rise in stock prices over one week
That is a market movement, not a recession.
A period in which prices fall for one product
That is a price change for one good.
A time when the government collects extra taxes
That is a revenue event.

q: What is a business cycle?
r: The repeating pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity
Phases include expansion, peak, contraction and trough.
w: The steps a company follows to make one product
That is a production process.
The yearly calendar of a company's sales events
That is a sales calendar.
The path of money from a bank to a borrower
That is lending.

q: During the expansion phase of the business cycle, what generally happens?
r: Output, employment and income grow
The economy moves toward a peak.
w: Output, employment and income all fall
That describes a contraction.
The economy stops producing goods
Production continues.
Prices become fixed by law
Prices are not fixed in an expansion.

q: What is the lowest point of a business cycle called?
r: The trough
After the trough, the economy begins to recover.
w: The peak
The peak is the highest point.
The expansion
That is a rising phase.
The equilibrium
That refers to market balance.

q: What is productivity?
r: The amount of output produced per unit of input, such as per hour of labor
Higher productivity raises living standards.
w: The total number of workers in a company
That is workforce size.
The wages paid to each worker
That is compensation.
The price at which goods are sold
That is price.

q: Which change would most directly increase labor productivity?
r: Giving workers better equipment and training
Capital and skills let each worker produce more.
w: Making workers stay at work for longer hours with no extra tools
More hours without tools adds fatigue.
Reducing the number of machines in the factory
Fewer machines usually lowers output.
Cutting worker training budgets
Less training usually lowers output per hour.

q: What is specialization?
r: Focusing on producing a limited range of goods or tasks
It lets people become more efficient.
w: Making every product in a single workshop
That is the opposite of focusing.
Buying goods only from foreign suppliers
That concerns trade.
Hiring workers who have no skills
Specialization builds skills.

q: What is division of labor?
r: Splitting production into separate tasks done by different workers
It increases output through specialization.
w: Dividing the profits among all shareholders
That is a profit split.
Splitting a large company into two firms
That is a corporate breakup.
Giving all workers identical jobs
That is the opposite.

q: What is the main purpose of money as a medium of exchange?
r: To make buying and selling easier than bartering
Everyone accepts it in payment.
w: To make goods impossible to trade
Money makes trade easier.
To ensure prices never change
Money does not fix prices.
To replace all work with leisure
Money does not replace work.

q: Which function of money lets people save purchasing power for later?
r: Store of value
Money can be held and spent in the future.
w: Medium of exchange
That lets money be used in trades.
Unit of account
That measures prices in a common unit.
Standard of deferred payment
That allows debts to be settled later.

q: What is inflation?
r: A general rise in the level of prices over time
Each dollar buys less than before.
w: A general fall in the level of prices over time
That describes deflation.
A rise in the price of one single product
Inflation is economy-wide.
An increase in the number of jobs
That is employment growth.

q: If prices rise by 5% in a year while a worker's pay rises by 2%, what happens to the worker's purchasing power?
r: It falls, because prices grew faster than pay
The worker can buy less than before.
w: It rises, because pay increased
Pay grew less than prices.
It stays the same, because both increased
Different rates change purchasing power.
It doubles, because both are positive
There is no such effect.

q: What is deflation?
r: A general decline in the level of prices over time
Money can buy more than before.
w: A general rise in the level of prices
That is inflation.
A fall in the supply of money to zero
That is not deflation.
A rise in the number of unemployed workers
That is unemployment.

q: What is unemployment?
r: The condition of people who are able and willing to work but cannot find jobs
They are counted among those actively looking.
w: The condition of people who choose to stay home and not look for work
They are not counted as unemployed.
The condition of people who work part-time by choice
Those workers are employed.
The condition of people who are retired
Retirees are not in the labor force.

q: A factory closes because consumers switched to a new technology and its workers must find jobs in other industries. What type of unemployment is this?
r: Structural unemployment
Skills no longer match available jobs.
w: Frictional unemployment
That is short-term job searching.
Cyclical unemployment
That is caused by recessions.
Seasonal unemployment
That is caused by the time of year.

q: A ski instructor is out of work every summer. What type of unemployment is this?
r: Seasonal unemployment
It follows the pattern of the seasons.
w: Structural unemployment
That arises from lasting economic shifts.
Frictional unemployment
That is a short gap between jobs.
Cyclical unemployment
That is caused by recessions.

q: What is an economic system?
r: The way a society decides what, how and for whom to produce
Every society must answer these basic questions.
w: The list of taxes that a country charges
Taxes are only one tool.
The set of machines used in a factory
That is capital equipment.
The rules of a single company's board
That is corporate governance.

q: Which three basic questions does every economic system answer?
r: What to produce, how to produce it and for whom
These are the core economic questions.
w: When to tax, whom to fine and where to build
These are not the basic questions.
Who to hire, where to advertise and what to charge
These are business questions.
Which bank to use, how to save and when to retire
These are personal finance questions.

q: In a market economy, who mainly decides what gets produced?
r: Consumers and producers acting through prices and competition
Individual choices guide the economy.
w: A central government planning office
That describes a command economy.
A royal family or tribal leader
That describes a traditional economy.
A foreign trade agency
That is not how a market economy decides.

q: In a command economy, who makes most economic decisions?
r: The central government
Planners decide what, how much and for whom.
w: Individual consumers
That describes a market economy.
Local families by custom
That describes a traditional economy.
Competing private firms
That describes a market economy.

q: What is a traditional economy?
r: An economy in which customs and habits guide production and trade
Roles are often handed down across generations.
w: An economy in which a central plan sets every price
That describes a command economy.
An economy in which only exports are allowed
That is not a traditional economy.
An economy in which computers make all decisions
That is not a traditional economy.

q: What is a mixed economy?
r: An economy that combines private choice with government involvement
Most modern economies are mixed.
w: An economy with no private firms at all
That would be a pure command economy.
An economy with no government role at all
That would be a pure market economy.
An economy based only on bartering
That is a traditional or barter system.

q: The United States is best described as which type of economic system?
r: A mixed economy that is mostly market-based
Private firms dominate, with government regulation.
w: A pure command economy
The government does not plan all production.
A traditional economy
Custom does not run production.
A barter economy
Money is used widely.

q: What is capitalism?
r: An economic system in which private owners control the means of production
Profit and competition drive decisions.
w: A system in which the government owns all property
That describes communism or state ownership.
A system in which people trade only by custom
That describes a traditional economy.
A system in which prices are set by law only
That describes a controlled economy.

q: What is socialism?
r: A system in which the government or community owns major industries
Goals include reducing inequality.
w: A system in which individuals own all businesses
That describes capitalism.
A system in which no taxes are collected
That is not socialism.
A system in which trade is banned
That is not socialism.

q: What is the role of profit in a market economy?
r: It rewards risk-taking and signals where resources are most wanted
Firms move toward profitable uses.
w: It guarantees that every business will succeed
Profit is not guaranteed.
It is set by the government for each firm
Profit is not set by government.
It is banned by law
Profit is allowed.
